opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something we've thought about a fair amount, and my take is that it's a useful signal but a pretty noisy one, and the noise matters in ways that are easy to miss.

The intuition is appealing. If a task pays a lot, presumably it's hard, takes a lot of skill or time, and so maybe AI systems will get to it later. But wages bundle together a lot of things that aren't really "difficulty" in the sense that matters for AI. Some of what you're paying for is scarcity of credentials, liability and trust, physical presence, regulatory barriers, bargaining power, or just the fact that the person's time is tied up for a long stretch. None of those map cleanly onto whether a model can actually do the cognitive work.

There's also the Moravec's paradox issue. A lot of low-wage work is physically and perceptually demanding in ways that have historically been really hard for AI and robotics, while some fairly well-paid work, like certain kinds of writing, coding, or analysis, turned out to be more tractable than people expected. So if you ranked tasks by wage and predicted automation order from that, you'd get some important things backwards.

That's part of why, in our work, we've leaned on a different proxy: how long a task takes a skilled human to complete. The time it takes someone with relevant expertise is closer to the thing we care about. It roughly tracks how many steps are involved, how much context you need to hold, and how many chances there are to go off the rails. And empirically it has turned out to be a pretty good predictor of whether current models succeed. Success rates fall off fairly smoothly as human completion time grows, which lets us talk about a model's "time horizon."

Even that isn't perfect. Human time is shaped by things like typing speed or familiarity with tools, and tasks can be messy in ways that don't show up in duration. Real-world work often has unclear specifications, needs you to gather context, or lacks a clean feedback signal, and our benchmark tasks tend to be cleaner than that. So I'd treat both wages and human time as rough proxies. But if you're asking which one I'd trust more for predicting what AI can do next, I'd go with something like task length plus some measure of messiness over market price. Wages tell you a lot about where the economic impact will be once a capability exists, which is a separate and also important question. They're just less informative about when that capability shows up.

r001.rationale: The response explains that low-wage physical and perceptual work can be difficult for AI, while some higher-paid cognitive work has been more tractable, so wages can misrank which tasks AI can perform.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a fair amount, partly because of the work we did on GPQA and then later on the METR-style stuff looking at how long tasks are that models can do. The basic idea is pretty appealing: if you want to know whether a model can automate some chunk of work, you look at what people get paid to do it, because the price of labor is kind of this aggregate signal about how hard the task is, how much expertise it requires, how scarce the people who can do it are. And it's nice because it's an existing measure, you don't have to invent it, the economy has already done the work of pricing things.

But I think it's a pretty unreliable predictor, and the reason is that the price of human labor is tracking the difficulty of the task for humans, which is just a different thing from the difficulty for AI systems. Those two things are correlated, but they come apart in ways that matter a lot. The classic example is something like Moravec's paradox: a radiologist is very expensive, a janitor is relatively cheap, and it turns out that reading a chest X-ray is the kind of thing where you can get a lot of leverage from pattern matching over a big dataset, whereas folding laundry in someone's messy apartment is still really hard for a robot. So the labor market says one of those tasks is much harder than the other, and from the point of view of the AI system it's sort of the reverse.

The other issue is that wages are bundling together a bunch of things that aren't really about the cognitive task at all. Part of what you're paying a lawyer for is liability, or credentialing, or the fact that someone has to be accountable if things go wrong. Part of what you're paying a doctor for is the bottleneck of residency slots. None of that is a property of the task itself. So if you naively use the price, you'll predict that AI should struggle with things that it actually finds easy, just because the humans who do them are expensive for institutional reasons.

And then there's the flip side, which is that a lot of the things models are weirdly bad at are cheap for humans. Like, keeping track of a long-horizon plan over days, noticing when you've made a mistake and backing up, dealing with an environment that doesn't give you clean feedback. Those aren't things that command a high wage, they're just things that basically every working adult does. But they're exactly the capabilities that seem to be the bottleneck right now.

So where I've landed is that labor price is a reasonable prior, and it's a useful sanity check, especially if you're trying to think about economic impact rather than capabilities per se. But if what you actually want is to predict what models can do, I think you have to look more directly at properties of the task: how long it is, how much context it requires, how verifiable the output is, whether there's training data that looks like it. Those things explain a lot more of the variance than the wage does. And honestly, I think a lot of the reason people reach for the labor-price framing is that it's legible and it maps onto conversations about jobs, not because it's actually the best predictor we have.

r001.rationale: The response says labor prices track task difficulty for humans, which differs from difficulty for AI, and illustrates the mismatch with radiology and laundry tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s useful to distinguish two questions: how economically valuable is a task, and how hard is it for an AI system to do? The price of human labor tells you something about the first, but it’s a pretty indirect signal about the second.

For example, a task might pay well because very few people have the training or credentials to do it. That doesn’t necessarily mean it’s difficult for a model to learn. And there are tasks that humans do fairly cheaply that require interacting with the physical world or handling a lot of implicit context, which can be quite difficult for AI systems.

So I’d be cautious about treating wages as a ranking of which tasks will be automated first. They can help you decide which capabilities are worth measuring, but you still want to test whether the system can actually perform the task, at the level of reliability that the job requires.

r001.rationale: The response explains that wages can reflect human credentials rather than AI difficulty, while low-paid physical or context-heavy tasks can still be hard for AI, so labor prices may not predict AI capability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s a pretty noisy proxy. The wage someone gets paid reflects a lot more than how difficult their job is for an AI system. It reflects supply and demand, how much training the person needed, and institutional factors. And a job is usually a bundle of tasks, some of which might be quite easy to automate while others are very difficult.

There’s also a distinction between whether an AI can do a task and whether it’s economical to use it for that task. The price of human labor is directly relevant to the second question, but it doesn’t necessarily tell you much about the first. A highly paid person might spend part of their day doing something a current model can do, while a relatively low-paid person might be doing physical work that’s still very challenging to automate.

So I’d want to look at the actual tasks and measure performance on those, rather than infer capabilities from wages alone.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts tasks a current model can do despite being part of highly paid work with low-paid physical work that remains challenging to automate, showing that AI and human capability profiles differ in ways wages do not capture.
